part_text: (-1) The European Parliament welcomes the Commission's proposal for fully updated employment guidelines for the Member States, in particular its focus on job quality, education and skills, new technologies, artificial intelligence and algorithmic management, poverty reduction, affordable housing and tackling labour and skills shortages. The European Parliament, with a view to strengthening democratic decision-making, reiterates its call to be involved in setting the Integrated Guidelines at Union level on an equal footing with the Council, in line with its legislative resolutions of 8 July 20151a, 19 April 20181b, 10 July 20201c, 18 October 20221d, 23 October 20241e and 8 October 20251f on the relevant proposals for Council decisions on guidelines for the employment policies of the Member States. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 1a Texts adopted, P8\_TA(2015)0201 (OJ C 265, 11.8.2017, p. 201). 1b Texts adopted, P8\_TA(2018)0181 (OJ C 390, 18.11.2019, p. 196). 1c Texts adopted, P9\_TA(2020)0194 (OJ 371, 15.9.2021, p. 134). 1d Texts adopted, P9\_TA(2022)0359 (OJ 149, 28.4.2023, p. 62). 1e Texts adopted, P10\_TA(2024)0027 (OJ C, C/2025/493, 29.1.2025, ELI:[http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/493/oj](http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/493/oj)). 1f Texts adopted, P10\_TA(2025)0217 (OJ C, C/2026/1548, 15.4.2026, ELI:[http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/1548/oj](http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/1548/oj)). / (1) Member States and the Union are to work towards developing a coordinated strategy for employment and in particular for the promotion of quality employment and improving working conditions, a skilled, trained and adaptable workforce, as well as inclusive and resilient labour markets, with a view to achieving the objectives of full employment and social progress, balanced economic growth and a highly competitive social market economy, a high level of protection and improvement of the quality of the environment laid down in Article 3 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). Member States are to regard promoting employment as a matter of common concern and to coordinate their action in that respect within the Council. / (2) The Union is to combat social exclusion and discrimination, promote social justice and protection and equality between women and men, close the gender pay and pension gaps, and foster solidarity between generations and the protection of the rights of the child as laid down in Article 3 TEU. In defining and implementing its policies and activities, the Union is to take into account requirements linked to the promotion of a high level of employment, the guarantee of adequate social protection, the fight against social exclusion, and a high level of education, training and protection of human health and dignity, as laid down in Article 9 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). Access to decent, sustainable and affordable housing, including through public and social housing, is a necessary condition for ensuring equal opportunities and social inclusion. / (3) In accordance with the TFEU, the Union has developed and implemented an integrated policy coordination framework for economic and employment policies in the context of the European Semester (4). The European Semester is aligned with the Competitiveness Compass, which provides a framework to boost competitiveness by closing the innovation gap, decarbonising our economy, reducing excessive dependencies and increasing security. The Compass identifies skills, quality jobs and social fairness among the horizontal enablers, which are essential to achieving the Compass’s three pillars and addressing skills and labour shortages hampering growth4a. The European Semester also integrates the principles of the European Pillar of Social Rights, proclaimed by the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission in November 2017 (5). It relies on the Social Scoreboard as its monitoring tool. The Social Scoreboard also provides the basis for an analysis of risks and challenges to upward social convergence in the Union, in the framework of the Social Convergence Framework (6). The European Semester provides for strong engagement with social partners, civil society and other stakeholders, and supports the delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals set out by the United Nations. The Semester is also complemented by the Digital Decade Policy Programme governance and recommendations. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2024 on the effective coordination of economic policies and on multilateral budgetary surveillance and repealing Council Regulation (EC) No 1466/97 (OJ L, 2024/1263, 30.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1263/oj). 4a Draghi, Mario, “The future of European competitiveness” (2025); Letta, Enrico “Much more than a market” (2024). 5 Interinstitutional Proclamation on the European Pillar of Social Rights (OJ C 428, 13.12.2017, p. 10). 6 See Art. 3(3)b and recital 8 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2024. / (5) The Employment Guidelines are consistent with the revised economic governance framework, the Social Convergence Framework and the implementation of the European Pillar of Social Rights and the Union headline targets for 2030. They are consistent with existing Union legislation and Union initiatives. These include inter alia the Commission Communications on the Union of Skills, of 5 March 2025 (9), on a Quality Jobs Roadmap of 4 December 2025, and on the European Union’s Anti-Poverty Strategy: addressing and preventing poverty from childhood to old age, and on Breaking the intergenerational cycle of child poverty: strengthening the European Child Guarantee, of 6 May 2026, as well as the Council Recommendations on Human Capital in the European Union of 9 March 2026, and on the European Pillar of Social Rights of 22 July 2026. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 8 Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2024 on the effective coordination of economic policies and on multilateral budgetary surveillance and repealing Council Regulation (EC) No 1466/97 (OJ L, 2024/1263, 30.4.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1263/oj). 9 COM(2025) 90 final. / (6) The European Pillar of Social Rights acts as the Union’s social shield and compass for fairness in an age of rapid transformations and challenges to protect and empower citizens. It sets out twenty principles and rights to support well-functioning and fair labour markets and welfare systems. They are structured around equal opportunities and access to the labour market, fair working conditions, and social protection and inclusion. These principles and rights give strategic direction to the Union, guiding continued action in the employment and social policy field and ensuring that the transitions to climate-neutrality, environmental sustainability and digitalisation are socially fair and just and contribute to social and territorial cohesion. The European Pillar of Social Rights, with its accompanying Social Scoreboard, also constitutes guidance to monitor the employment, skills and social performance of Member States and upward social convergence in the Union, in the European Semester. The Pillar drives reforms and investments at national, regional and local levels, supporting a competitive social market economy in today’s modern economy, including by promoting the social economy. / (7) On 4 March 2021, the Commission put forward an Action Plan for the implementation of the European Pillar of Social Rights. This included ambitious yet realistic Union headline targets for 2030 on employment (at least 78% of the population aged 20-64 should be in employment), skills (at least 60% of all adults should participate in training every year) and poverty reduction (at least 15 million fewer people should be at risk of poverty or social exclusion, including 5 million children) (the ‘Union headline targets for 2030’). It also included complementary sub-targets, as well as a revised Social Scoreboard. As recognised by the Heads of State or Government at the Porto Social Summit on 8 May 2021, the implementation of the European Pillar of Social Rights will strengthen the Union’s drive towards a digital, green and fair transition and contribute to achieving upward social and economic convergence and addressing demographic challenges. The Heads of State or Government stressed that the social dimension, social dialogue and the active involvement of social partners are at the core of a highly competitive social market economy. The Union headline targets for 2030 were welcomed by the Heads of State or Government at the Porto Social Summit of May 2021 and by the June 2021 European Council. They support, together with the Social Scoreboard, the monitoring of progress towards the implementation of the principles of the European Pillar of Social Rights in the European Semester. Against this background, Member States also set ambitious national targets which, taking due account of the starting position of each Member State, constitute an adequate contribution to the achievement of the three Union headline targets for 2030. / (9) The Integrated Guidelines serve as a basis for the country-specific recommendations addressed by the Council to Member States under the European Semester. While the Integrated Guidelines are addressed to Member States and the Union, they should be implemented in partnership with all national, regional and local authorities, closely involving parliaments, as well as social partners and representatives of civil society. Labour market and social reforms should fully respect national practices of social dialogue and collective bargaining, as well as the autonomy of social partners. The importance of social dialogue in tackling challenges in the world of work was reaffirmed at the 2024 Val Duchesse Summit and in the Pact for European Social Dialogue signed in March 2025. Member States should ensure the transposition and effective implementation of the Directive (EU) 2022/2041 of the European Parliament and of the Council1a and prepare and implement collective-bargaining action plans where required by Article 4 of that Directive as well as the complete transposition and implementation of Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council1b. Such implementation should take into account national, regional and sectoral labour-market conditions, including persistent shortages and surpluses, demographic challenges, braindrain and the specific needs of SMEs. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 1a* *Directive (EU) 2022/2041 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union (OJ L 275, 25.10.2022, pp. 33). 1b* *Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 to strengthen the application of the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value between men and women through pay transparency and enforcement mechanisms (OJ L 132, 17.5.2023, p. 21). / (10) Member States should make full use of available EU funding, in particular the European Social Fund Plus and the Social Climate Fund, Just Transition Fund and the future MFF, to foster quality employment and skills, help fight poverty and support employment and social reforms and investments. This includes fighting social exclusion, combatting discrimination, ensuring accessibility and inclusion, particularly for people with disabilities and marginalised groups such as Roma, and promoting upskilling and reskilling opportunities for the workforce, lifelong learning and high-quality education and training for all. Investment in skills should take account of identified labour-market needs and structural shortages and support high-quality vocational education and training, apprenticeships and effective transitions into employment. Union funding should also support measures to adapt workplaces and working conditions to climate-related risks. Climate change and the increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, including heatwaves, floods and other climate-related hazards, such as wildfires, are already affecting working conditions, workers’ health and safety, well-being and productivity. For the funding period post-2027, the National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs), in particular the European Social Fund and the Competitiveness Fund, will continue promoting and strengthening integrated efforts in these areas. In the context of the overarching decarbonisation objectives of the Union, the Social Climate Fund (10) will be key in addressing the needs of vulnerable households, vulnerable transport users and vulnerable micro-enterprises. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 10 Regulation (EU) 2023/955 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 establishing a Social Climate Fund and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1060 (OJ L 130, 16.5.2023, p. 1-51). / Guideline 5: Boosting quality job creation / To strengthen resilience in the face of possible economic, labour-market and climate-related shocks, well-designed short-time work schemes, such as the SURE programme, and similar arrangements can, together with targeted training, help workers to remain employed during temporary downturns and companies’ restructuring while facilitating the dynamic reallocation of labour in the economy. Well-designed hiring and transition incentives and upskilling and reskilling measures, lifelong learning and VET, developed in close cooperation with social partners, can also support structural transformations by facilitating restructuring processes and the reallocation of labour from declining sectors towards emerging ones, while safeguarding employment, wages, working conditions and acquired rights. They can therefore help to preserve employment and to modernise the economy, including via associated skills development. Employment-protection instruments modelled on SURE and Just Transition funding should be reinforced. Proactive employment support should cover transferable upskilling and reskilling and job-to-job transitions. / In the context of the digital and green transitions, demographic change, persisting inequalities and geopolitical shifts, and the importance of security and defence, together with the related need for greater strategic autonomy of the Union, including with regards to technological sovereignty, Member States should promote sustainability, inclusiveness, competitiveness, productivity, employability and the acquisition of skills and competences throughout people's lives, responding to current and future labour market needs. They should address skills and labour shortages, including through better and timelier skills intelligence, also in light of the Union and national skills headline targets for 2030. Member States should also modernise and invest in their education, and training systems, also in rural and remote areas, and including related infrastructure, such as VET centres aligned with the regional economies, to provide high quality, accessible and inclusive education and training, and stimulate increased upskilling and reskilling. This should also ensure that the workforce has the right skills to develop and deploy solutions in view of the fast-changing deep tech and clean industry development. Member States should work together with social partners, education and training providers, enterprises and other stakeholders to address structural weaknesses in their education and training systems and, in particular, support SMEs to recruit, train and retain qualified workers. Decent working conditions - including fair wages, standard employment contracts, social protection, lifelong learning, occupational safety and health, work-life balance, reasonable working time, workers' representation, democracy at work and collective bargaining - are crucial to attracting and retaining skilled workers. / To enhance employability and quality job creation and transitions, Member States should ensure an effective individual right to accessible, quality education and training during working time and at no cost to the worker. Such a right can include, where appropriate, individual learning accounts, reliable training quality assessments and micro-credentials. They should enable everyone to anticipate and better adapt to labour market needs, in particular through continuous upskilling and reskilling and the provision of integrated career guidance and counselling. Member States should raise awareness, including among employers, of the importance of lifelong-learning-friendly work, and ensure that employment, skills, industrial and investment policies are mutually reinforcing and informed by reliable labour-market intelligence. They should also support the reallocation of workers towards sectors and occupations with stronger employment prospects, while taking into account regional and sectoral shortages and the specific challenges of rural, peripheral and less-developed regions affected by ageing, outward migration and a declining working-age population. Member States should ensure that all formal qualifications and credentials offer clear pathways for further studies or progression. / Member States should provide unemployed and inactive people with effective, timely, coordinated and tailor-made assistance based on support for job searches, upskilling and reskilling and access to other enabling services, paying particular attention to vulnerable groups and people affected by the green and digital transitions. Comprehensive strategies that include in-depth individual assessments of unemployed people and validation of prior work experience should be pursued as soon as possible, with a view to significantly reducing and preventing long-term unemployment. Youth unemployment and the challenge of young people not in employment, education or training (NEETs) should continue to be addressed through prevention of early leaving from education and training and improvement of the school-to-work transition, alongside the full implementation of the reinforced Youth Guarantee, notably by making an offer within 4 months for young people aged 15-29, to guarantee early intervention, and by providing support for quality youth-employment opportunities. / Member States should remove barriers and disincentives to, and provide incentives for, labour market participation, in particular for low-income earners, second earners (often women), older people, persons with disabilities, and those furthest from the labour market, including people with a migrant background and Roma. Member States should contribute to fostering labour supply and address shortages, improving wages and working conditions, ensuring that the design of tax and benefit systems promote adequate income protection and a dignified standard of living, and that active labour market policies are effective and accessible, respecting the role and autonomy of social partners. Member States should also support a work environment which ensures accessibility and reasonable accommodation for persons with disabilities, offering quality non-segregated employment and career progression, including through targeted financial and technical support, maintenance of disability allowances while employed, information and awareness raising, and services that enable them to participate in the labour market and in society. The social economy can play a key role in securing quality jobs for persons with disabilities. The Disability Employment Package under the Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2021-2030, as enhanced by the Commission Communication of 6 May 2026, should be fully implemented in workplaces, with particular attention to retention strategies and elimination of discriminatory practices. / Member States should ensure gender equality and increased labour market participation of women, including in relation to career progression, by tackling gender stereotypes as well as gender-segmented labour markets and systematic gender gaps in access to relevant education and training, eliminating barriers to leadership access at all levels of decision making, ensuring paid maternity and parental leave for all parents and effectively implementing Directive (EU) 2022/2381 of the European Parliament and of the Council1a, and pursuing equivalent measures in the public sector. Member States must tackle workplace violence and harassment, in line with ILO Convention 190 on violence and harassment in the world of work. Member States should also transpose and effectively implement Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council1b., to ensure equal pay for equal work, or work of equal value, and pay transparency should be ensured. The reconciliation of work, family and private life for both women and men should be promoted, in particular through access to affordable, high quality long-term care and early childhood education and care. Member States should ensure that parents and other people with caring responsibilities have access to suitable and paid family-related leave and flexible working arrangements to balance work, family and private life, and promote a balanced use of those entitlements between parents. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 1a. Directive (EU) 2022/2381 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 November 2022 on improving the gender balance among directors of listed companies and related measures (OJ L 315, 7.12.2022, p. 44, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2381/oj). 1b. Directive (EU) 2023/970 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 to strengthen the application of the principle of equal pay for equal work or work of equal value between men and women through pay transparency and enforcement mechanisms (OJ L 132, 17.5.2023, p. 21, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/970/oj). / Member States should work together with social partners in ensuring fair, transparent and predictable working conditions. To enhance job quality, they should reduce and prevent segmentation in labour markets, fight undeclared work and bogus self-employment, including through cooperation between social security and labour inspection authorities, with particular attention to sectors and workers at higher risk of labour exploitation, including third-country national and mobile workers, and foster the transition towards open-ended forms of employment. Workplace well-being and job autonomy should be promoted as contributing to job quality. Member States should, in accordance with Principle No 5 of the European Pillar of Social Rights, prevent employment relationships that lead to precarious working conditions, including by prohibiting the abuse of atypical contracts. Employment protection rules, labour law and institutions should protect labour rights, provide access to social protection, enable inclusive recruitment and ensure safe, healthy, climate-resilient and well-adapted work environments for all workers, while providing necessary flexibility for companies to adapt to changes. To strengthen the effective enforcement of labour law, Member States should ensure that labour inspectorates are adequately staffed, sufficiently resourced and operationally equipped to carry out regular inspections in accordance with national practices and ILO conventions. Promoting the use of flexible working arrangements such as teleworking can contribute to higher employment levels and more inclusive labour markets, including for previously excluded groups, but it can also blur the boundary between working time and private life. Member States should address gaps in social protection coverage for workers who temporarily lose work and income due to extreme weather events. / Member States should support workers and employers in the digital transformation, including through the effective, responsible, inclusive and ethical human-centric use of AI tools that boost productivity and complement human labour. Member States should take concrete measures to ensure that increasing AI-driven automation does not lead to a reduction in labour’s share of income, which would not only increase inequalities but could also weaken aggregate demand, investment and economic growth. To foster a trust-based approach to workplace technology and innovation, Member States should also monitor impacts on the labour market functioning, including recruitment practices, and leverage the role of social dialogue and collective bargaining. Member States should further adapt education and training pathways to the changing impact of AI across occupations and resulting shifts in occupational demand, including by raising the profile and attractiveness of VET professions that are less susceptible to AI-related disruption. Precarious working conditions should be prevented, including in platform work, atypical work contracts and work mediated through intermediaries, by ensuring fairness, transparency, non-discrimination and human accountability in the use of algorithms, and by fighting abusive contractual arrangements. To this end, Member States should ensure timely and complete transposition and effective enforcement of Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council1a. Access to effective, impartial dispute resolution and a right to redress, including adequate compensation, where applicable, should be ensured in cases of unfair dismissal. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ 1a. Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on improving working conditions in platform work (OJ L, 2024/2831, 11.11.2024, ELI:[http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2831/oj](http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2831/oj)). / Member States should effectively activate and enable those who can participate in the labour market, especially underrepresented groups, such as women and young people, as well as people in vulnerable situations, such as the lower-skilled, the long-term unemployed, persons with disabilities, people with a migrant background, people from Roma communities and older workers. Member States should strengthen the scope and effectiveness of active labour market policies by increasing their availability, outreach and coverage and by better linking them with social services, training and income support for the unemployed. Member States should enhance the capacity of public employment services to provide timely and tailor-made assistance to jobseekers, including through performance-based management and better capacity to use data and digital technology, and by making the best use of Union funding as well as national resources. / Member States should also strive to create the appropriate conditions for new forms of work, and working methods, delivering on their job creation potential while ensuring full compliance with Union and national law. They should enforce applicable rules in the context of atypical contracts and new forms of work, such as work through digital labour platforms. In this regard, social partners can play an instrumental role and Member States should support them in reaching out to and representing people in atypical and new forms of work. Member States should also strengthen enforcement through adequate capacities and dedicated training for labour inspectorates, concerning the challenges stemming from new forms of work, including the use of digital technologies and AI, such as algorithmic management, workers’ surveillance and telework, working conditions and occupational safety and health, particularly psychosocial health. Effective enforcement of workers' rights and labour law are key in the context of digitalisation, and in the use of AI and algorithmic management at the workplace. / Member States should foster democracy at work and ensure an enabling environment for bipartite and tripartite social dialogue at all levels, including collective bargaining, in the public and private sectors, in accordance with national law and/or practice, after consultation and in close cooperation with social partners, while respecting their autonomy. Member States should involve social partners in a systematic, meaningful and timely manner in the design and implementation of employment, social and, where relevant, economic and other public policies, including in the setting and updating of statutory minimum wages. Member States should promote higher collective bargaining coverage, with the aim of achieving a collective bargaining coverage rate of 80%, in line with the objective set out in Directive (EU) 2022/2041, including by strengthening social partners’ capacity, enable effective collective bargaining at all appropriate levels and encourage coordination between and across those levels. Social partners should be encouraged to negotiate and conclude collective agreements in matters relevant to them, fully respecting their autonomy and the right to collective action. Where relevant, and building on existing national practices, Member States should take into account the relevant experience of civil society organisations on employment and social issues, given their first-hand knowledge of how services and systems operate in practice on the ground. / Particular attention should be given to fighting poverty, including in-work poverty, and social exclusion, in a life cycle perspective from childhood to old age, in line with the Union and national poverty reduction headline targets for 2030 and the aim of eradicating poverty by 2035 through progress indicators and clear milestones. Member States should have effective anti-poverty policy frameworks in line with the Union’s Anti-Poverty Strategy and address social mobility and intergenerational and multi-dimensional challenges. With a view to further preventing and addressing poverty, discrimination and stigma, difficulties to afford basic needs, such as food, energy, a home and other basic goods, and the lack of access to quality services, should be tackled. Member States should recognise that the lack of decent, sustainable and affordable housing can impede access to employment, labour mobility and the retention of workers. Member States should develop and integrate the three strands of active inclusion (adequate income support, inclusive labour markets and access to quality enabling services) to meet individual needs. Social protection and inclusion systems should ensure adequate minimum income benefits for everyone lacking sufficient resources and promote social inclusion by supporting and encouraging people in working age to participate in the labour market and society, including through targeted provision of social services. Member States should ensure that everyone has access to essential services of good quality. The availability of universally accessible, affordable and quality services, such as early childhood education and care, out-of-school care, education, training, housing, health and long-term care, is a necessary condition for ensuring equal opportunities, including by alleviating food and material deprivation. To break the cycle of disadvantage, child poverty and social exclusion should be especially addressed by comprehensive and integrated measures, including through the full implementation of the European Child Guarantee, with a particular focus on single-parent households, the large majority of which are headed by women, and to the compounded risks faced by women in old age, migrant women and women with disabilities. / Member States should ensure access to decent, affordable and sustainable housing, including public or social housing. Mobilising private and public investments for affordable and social housing, in a context where other supply bottlenecks are also addressed, will be key to achieve progress. In addition, Member States should provide well targeted housing assistance and other support measures, for people in need or in a vulnerable situation. Social economy housing providers, innovative financing models and targeted measures to mobilise vacant housing can be building blocks towards sustainable and inclusive housing solutions. Energy and transport poverty, as well as resilience to health risks and disasters, including those triggered by climate change and environmental degradation, should be addressed with targeted support measures for low-income households and disadvantaged groups. Member States should also ensure that the loss of a primary residence through enforcement proceedings is solely a measure of last resort. Member States should make effective use of Union funding to invest in affordable and social housing, student housing, housing renovation and accompanying services. The specific needs of persons with disabilities, including accessibility, should be taken into account, including in the provision of affordable and social housing particularly as regards new builds and renovation of existing housing stock. Homelessness and housing exclusion should be tackled specifically by boosting the supply of affordable and social housing, prevention measures and promoting an inclusive, people-centred housing-led and integrated approach, particularly through the housing first principle, to ensure that support meets real needs. / In a context of increasing longevity and demographic change, Member States should secure the adequacy and sustainability of pension systems for workers and the self-employed, providing equal opportunities for women and men to acquire and accrue pension rights, including through supplementary schemes to ensure a decent retirement income above the poverty line. Pension reforms should be supported by policies that aim to reduce the gender pension gap, including by adequately valued periods of maternity and parental leave, and to promote active and healthy ageing and decent working conditions to ensure that workers can actually remain in employment until they reach the statutory retirement age. At the same time workers who wish to remain active after they have reached the retirement age should have the possibility to do so. Member States should establish a constructive dialogue with social partners and other relevant stakeholders and allow for an appropriate phasing in of the reforms. Part-time and non-standard workers should have equitable access to supplementary pension schemes. Member States should promote transparency of pension rights, including through pension tracking services. / Member States should ensure timely access to affordable, preventive and curative healthcare of good quality, including mental health services, while safeguarding sustainability in the long term. In the context of an increasing demand for long-term care, also linked to demographic change, gaps in adequacy and availability of services, labour shortages, poor working conditions and often inadequate remuneration of carers should be addressed through comprehensive and integrated measures. Furthermore, Member States should work towards developing care models that are person-centred, ensure smooth transition between different care pathways (e.g. from hospital to home and/or residential care) and address health and long-term care needs in an integrated manner. Member States should ensure that unpaid and informal carers also have access to social protection, including pension credits, as well as adequate compensation, minimum respite periods, financial support and enabling services.
